questions: Do they occur repeatedly or intermittently rather than being continuously fixed?
Are they worsened by voluntary movement, stress, fatigue, or attempts to use the affected limbs?
Can lightly touching your face, neck, or another body part temporarily reduce the abnormal posture?
Does your head involuntarily turn, tilt, or pull backward or forward?
Are the neck muscles painful or unusually tight during or after these episodes?
Do you have involuntary shaking or jerking of the head or arms?
Are the upper-limb postures brought on specifically by writing, typing, playing an instrument, or another skilled activity?
Have the abnormal postures spread from one body region to other regions?
Have you noticed slowness, stiffness, balance problems, reduced arm swing, or a resting tremor?
Did these symptoms begin after taking an antipsychotic, anti-nausea medication, antidepressant, anticonvulsant, or other new medication?
Is there a family history of dystonia, abnormal involuntary movements, Parkinson disease, or similar symptoms?
Did the symptoms begin suddenly or after an injury, infection, or major psychological stress?
Do you have weakness, numbness, loss of coordination, difficulty speaking, swallowing problems, or changes in vision?
Have you had seizures, episodes of loss of awareness, or loss of bladder control?
Did the symptoms begin before age 26?
Do you have liver disease, psychiatric symptoms, or a history of excessive alcohol use?
Have you ever had similar abnormal postures in your legs, trunk, jaw, or face?

results: 1. Comprehensive movement-disorders neurological examination, including assessment for dystonia during rest, voluntary activation, distraction, dual-tasking, and gait
muscle tone examination: abnormal dystonic increased tone with severe retrocollis and bilateral upper limb dystonia
deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses: normal
posture and pull test: abnormal severe retrocollis; pull test preserved
distribution of the dystonia (focal, segmental, generalized): perioral dystonia, severe retrocollis from the upper back to the neck, and bilateral upper limb dystonia
action specificity and task dependence: not characterised
eye movements and reflexes: normal saccades and pursuit; normal deep tendon and plantar reflexes
2. Video recording of the abnormal postures during spontaneous activity, sustained voluntary movements, distraction, and attempted relaxation
3. Surface electromyography of the neck and upper-limb muscles during the abnormal postures and during voluntary movements
5. MRI of the cervical spinal cord
6. Serum ceruloplasmin, serum copper, and 24-hour urinary copper
copper / caeruloplasmin / 24 h urinary copper: normal
7. Complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, thyroid-stimulating hormone, vitamin B12, folate, and vitamin E
serum electrolytes, urea and creatinine: normal
full blood count and biochemistry: normal
8. Genetic testing for dystonia-associated variants, including TOR1A, THAP1, GNAL, and KMT2B
dystonia gene panel: pathogenic THAP1 variant c.505C>T (p.Arg169*), heterozygous - DYT6
9. A supervised diagnostic trial of botulinum toxin injections into clinically affected dystonic muscles
dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: THAP1-related dystonia (DYT6), an autosomal-dominant segmental dystonia caused by the heterozygous pathogenic THAP1 c.505C>T (p.Arg169*) truncating variant

ALTERNATIVE 1: Idiopathic segmental dystonia

ALTERNATIVE 2: Tardive or other acquired segmental dystonia

ALTERNATIVE 3: Functional dystonia
